first_impression.reaction: The first paragraph already names stuff I searched for: the bed, names on the shoe, sugared almonds, the circle dance. And the first takeaway, no vows, is actually a thing I didn't know. That's enough to stop me bouncing. The numbered 1 to 12 headings make it easy to scroll on the train.

journey.quote: The other is the family folklore around it: the bed made by friends, names on a shoe, sugared almonds in odd numbers, a circle dance that pulls in every generation.
journey.reaction: Good, answers are showing up in the first few lines. No long story about someone's yiayia before I get anything.

journey.quote: The Orthodox wedding service has no vows and centres on the crowning of the couple, not on a ring exchange or a kiss.
journey.reaction: Okay, that's the 'did not know' bit the title promised. I'd screenshot this one.

journey.quote: To marry legally in Greece, check with the Greek municipality and the Australian Embassy in Athens about a Certificate of No Impediment, an apostille and any fees, as at November 2026.
journey.reaction: I searched for traditions, not paperwork. This bullet takes up the last slot in the box I actually read. At least it's dated, so I know it's recent.

journey.quote: Tell your photographer and your guests that this, not the rings or a kiss, is the moment to watch.
journey.reaction: Useful and practical. If I'm a guest I now know when to look up from my phone.

journey.section: How long is a Greek Orthodox wedding service?
journey.quote: Your priest is the right person to ask about timing, since the length depends on the parish, the music and the size of the wedding party.
journey.reaction: The heading asks my exact question and then doesn't answer it. I don't have a priest. Even a rough 'usually around this long' would do. This is the one spot I felt baited.

journey.section: 12. The kalamatianos, the money dance and "Na zisete"
journey.quote: No one actually spits, and it is meant kindly.
journey.reaction: Ha, this is the one my friends would ask about. Clear and quick.

journey.quote: Plate smashing is the custom outsiders most associate with a Greek celebration, but it is not part of the wedding service, and many families never do it at a wedding.
journey.reaction: Honestly, this is the thing I most expected to read about, and it's down past tradition 12. Nice myth-bust though.

journey.section: Greek wedding traditions from ancient Greece
journey.quote: Encyclopaedias and museum collections describe the ancient customs, including the age at which girls married, in detail.
journey.reaction: So... what are they? The section ends right there. It feels like a placeholder. I'd rather it was cut than left like this.

journey.quote: "Na zisete", a wish for a long life together.
journey.reaction: Short, useful FAQ. The guest questions (what to wear, what to say, what to give) are exactly what someone invited to a Greek wedding would google.

unanswered_questions: Roughly how long does a Greek Orthodox wedding service usually last? The heading asks it but the answer is 'ask your priest'.
What were the actual ancient Greek wedding customs? The section names the topic but gives nothing.
What does rolling a baby across the krevati most commonly mean? The page only says families tell different stories.

would_share_with: A friend invited to a Greek wedding (the FAQ, the stefana moment and the ftou ftou bit)

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like to talk through the plans around the day, venues, guest travel and timing, a Wedded Advisor is glad to start that conversation.
cta_reaction.why: I'm here out of curiosity, not planning a wedding. It's low-key and there's nothing pushy or blocking the content, which I appreciate. I'd more likely tap the German or Turkish traditions links next.

top_3_changes: Answer the 'How long is a Greek Orthodox wedding service?' heading with a typical range, then add 'ask your priest', or drop the heading.
Either fill the ancient Greece section with real content or cut it; right now it reads like a placeholder.
Swap the legal-paperwork bullet in Key takeaways for a traditions one (plate smashing is a myth at most weddings, or ftou ftou), and keep the legal detail in its own section.
